title: Capacity assurance: buyers' journey, procurement signals, and seller scenarios
content:
Purpose:
This working brief maps buyer signals, recommended messaging, procurement-ready artifacts, and common seller scenarios for capacity-assurance offers (reserved inference / committed GPU pools). The aim is a compact playbook sellers can use during procurement cycles where customers prioritize SLAs, isolation, and predictable throughput rather than purely lowest unit cost.

Executive summary:
- Problem buyers tell us: we need predictable throughput, a clear SLA, and strong isolation guarantees for regulated or latency-sensitive inference workloads. They hate surprise throttling and ad-hoc model evictions.
- Positioning focus: sell capacity-as-assurance, not just hardware. Emphasize end-to-end incident liability (SLOs + compensatory credits), deterministic throughput curves, and network/data isolation options that make integration into security/compliance programs straightforward.
- Outcome for customer: applications that hit latency/throughput targets under load, with auditability and a clear remediation path if guarantees fail.

Buyer personas and key signals:
1) Platform architect (mid-market / enterprise)
   - Signals: RFP language around "dedicated endpoints", questions about isolation, references to multi-tenant risk.
   - What they care about: network segmentation (VPC, private link), KMS/HSM integrations, predictable QoS across peak windows.
   - Quick win message: "Reserved GPU pools + private control plane gives you deterministic throughput and simple SLA-backed remediation."

2) ML engineering lead
   - Signals: concerns about model eviction or CPU/GPU contention; requests for performance benchmarks at target sequence lengths and concurrency.
   - What they care about: consistent latency percentiles, ability to pin model versions, warm KV cache guarantees for steady-state traffic.
   - Quick win message: "We provide per-route latency profiles and can validate your prompt distribution in a pre-prod soak test before go-live."

3) Procurement / Legal
   - Signals: demands for monetary credits, clear uptime definitions, termination clauses tied to failure to meet SLAs.
   - What they care about: precise SLA language, audit rights, data residency, and termination/penalty mechanics.
   - Quick win message: "Standard SLA with tiered service credits, audit-friendly logs retained for X months, and optional SOC2/Pen test attachments."

Competitive nuances and rebuttals
- Cloud IaaS + self-hosting: buyers think they can DIY cheaper. Rebuttal: total cost of ownership for inference (ops, burst handling, KV cache warm-up, kernel tuning) and the time to reach required 99th pct latencies often exceeds expectations. Offer a side-by-side: measured throughput-cost with and without our runtime optimizations.
- Managed LLM API providers: some offer 'enterprise isolation', but many lack predictable throughput at scale. Rebuttal: demonstrate deterministic load tests and offer a buyer-validated soak plan (we run their workload profile on reserved capacity).
- Specialized inference vendors: deep technical comparators on quantization/latency. Rebuttal: focus on operational guarantees, fallback modes, and SLAs that cover the stack, not only the model runtime.

Procurement-ready artifacts to have ready
- SLA template (short): uptime target, latency percentile targets per route/model, service credits banding, exclusion clause list.
- Isolation spec: network architecture diagrams (VPC, private link, on-prem gateway), data handling commitments, KMS/HSM integration notes.
- Capacity Sizing worksheet (sheet): concurrency, average seq length, expected RPS, warm cache assumptions -> recommended reserved GPU count and burst buffer policy.
- Soak & validation plan (doc): timeline, success criteria, telemetry to collect, rollback triggers.
- Playbook for incident remediation and credit calculation (doc): how we validate breaches, timelines for credit issuance, and communication templates.

Sample SLA language (plain form sellers can paste into contract discussions)
- Availability: Redwood agrees to make Reserved Capacity available 99.95% monthly (excluding scheduled maintenance and force majeure).
- Latency: For primary reserved endpoints, median latency shall be <= X ms and 99th percentile <= Y ms for the agreed token/sequence profile.
- Credit model: If availability falls below SLA in a billing month, customer receives service credits equal to Z% of that month’s reserved capacity charge, escalated by missed tiers.
- Remediation obligations: Redwood will provide a root-cause summary within 5 business days and a remediation plan with milestones if SLA is missed.

Seller scenarios and scripts
1) Early discovery (demo / initial call)
   - Seller opener: "Tell me about your peak windows. Are there periodic batch spikes or steady, high-concurrency traffic?"
   - If buyer says 'we're nervous about noisy neighbors': "We offer reserved pools that eliminate multi-tenant interference and let you pin models and versions. We can run a performance test with your prompt set before you commit."

2) Procurement negotiating credits
   - Common ask: higher credits, lower uptime threshold.
   - Seller framing: "We can include a structured credit schedule tied to major SLA bands. For heavier financial guarantees, we offer an enhanced package (enterprise tier) that includes longer retention, increased runbook access, and a named escalation path."

3) Tech deep-dive with ML infra team
   - Runbook: bring the capacity sizing worksheet, a small benchmark run tailored to their token/seq distribution, and the isolation diagram. Offer to run the benchmark in their region to remove network variance.

Pre-sales soak test (recommended process)
- Phase 0: intake - collect representative prompts, expected concurrency, sequence length histogram.
- Phase 1: staging validation - run 24–72 hours on reserved nodes, collect latency percentiles, KV cache warm hits, and failure modes.
- Phase 2: pilot - limited production traffic with monitoring hooks, agreed ramp and rollback plan.
- Acceptance criteria: no more than X% request error rate, 99th percentile latency within agreed band for 95% of tests, no unapproved model evictions.

Risk and FAQ (short)
- Q: Can you guarantee no noisy neighbor impacts?
  A: The reserved pool isolates compute and scheduling; shared control plane remains but we commit to eviction policies that preserve reserved tenant throughput.
- Q: What about burst traffic above reserved baseline?
  A: We provide configurable burst capacity policies and a short-term burst buffer billed separately or consumed from a burst allowance; we also support prioritized routing to a compatible variant when capacity is saturated.
- Q: How do you validate SLA breaches?
  A: We use server-side telemetry, ingestion logs, and customer-provided traces when needed. Credits are calculated from telemetry and reconciled within the agreed SLA dispute window.

Open questions for legal/infra before broader roll-out
- Finalize default values for latency bands (X/Y ms) per model class.
- Decide on minimum notice and blackout windows for scheduled maintenance for reserved pools.
- Define audit support scope (on-site, remote log export, or both) and retention windows tied to tiers.

Next steps (for GTM and sales ops)
- Create a one-page SLA cheat sheet sellers can carry into procurement meetings.
- Build a template soak-run in our staging infra with a self-serve input form for customer prompt histograms.
- Align legal on two standard SLA packages (standard & enterprise) and the corresponding credit/penalty schedules.
- Train AE/SE on three role-play scenarios: architect objection, procurement credit push, and burst-case handling.

Appendix: short checklist for AE/SE before procurement call
- Have capacity sizing worksheet completed with customer numbers.
- Bring the isolation diagram for the chosen deployment mode (Hosted-dedicated / Dedicated-in-VPC / Private).
- Confirm which telemetry (logs, traces, metrics) the customer needs and retention tier.
- Offer to run a 48-hour soak test on reserved capacity as part of the pilot phase.

Document notes: this is intentionally a working playbook. Keep bullets compact and update after first three procurement cycles with revised latency numbers and real customer case studies.
